The ochre sea star Pisaster ochraceus begins its life as a planktonic bipinnaria larva, which commences planktotrophic feeding immediately upon hatching at a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The newly hatched larva, measured as the width of the larval body as a proxy for arm length, possesses a total length of approximately 0.02 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.02 centimeters], reflecting the tiny size typical of echinoderm propagules. This larval stage persists for a specific duration, with the time since birth at metamorphosis recorded as 150 days  under the same thermal regime. at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]Upon reaching metamorphic competence, the brachiolaria larva settles and undergoes a dramatic body plan reorganisation, resulting in a post-metamorphic juvenile with a total length of 0.22 centimeters . The progression from a free-swimming bilateral larva to a benthic juvenile is a critical allometric shift. During the initial larval feeding stage, the bipinnaria larva measures between 0.160 and 0.250 millimeters in width, which serves as the basis for the length-at-birth estimate. It is important to note that this larval width proxy is not the same measurement used for describing adult arm length, which is recorded from the center of the disk to the tip of the arm and can reach 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters].

The post-metamorphic juvenile experiences a prolonged period of somatic growth and gonad maturation before reaching reproductive capability. Based on field estimates, puberty in Pisaster ochraceus is attained at a total length of 5.9 centimeters [Lp = 5.9 centimeters], with individuals lacking gonads until they exceed a wet weight of 70 grams [Wwp = 70 grams]. This size threshold for the onset of gametogenesis is corroborated by observational studies from the early work of Menge and from Pearse and Eernisse. The time since birth at puberty, estimated under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], is 730 days [tp = 730 days]. This interval incorporates a 150-day larval period followed by a substantial juvenile growth phase. Field observations by Menge suggested a longer period of up to 5 years to reach reproductive maturity, but these are believed to reflect suboptimal foraging conditions in the intertidal environment. Under the consistent thermal conditions typical of a 13 °C regime, laboratory-reared juveniles achieve the critical weight of 70 grams [Wwp = 70 grams] on this accelerated timeline, demonstrating the importance of food availability and temperature for developmental rate.

As individuals continue to grow beyond the pubertal threshold, they attain an ultimate total length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters], which represents the maximum recorded arm length for the species from the center of the disk to the arm tip. This asymptotic size is accompanied by an ultimate wet weight that reaches 1200 grams [Wwi = 1200 grams] in large, well-fed adults occupying productive rocky intertidal habitats. The extraordinary longevity of this keystone predator is notable, with the lifespan extending to 34 years [am = 34 years] when maintained at a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This maximum lifespan of 34 years is consistent with the slow life-history pace observed in many large-bodied temperate asteroids and underscores the species' investment in durable somatic structures. The age at birth, defined as the time from fertilisation to hatching, is a mere 4.5 days [ab = 4.5 days] at 13 °C, marking a rapid developmental transition from the zygote stage to a free-swimming exogenously feeding larva at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This brief incubation period is characteristic of broadcast-spawning echinoderms that rely on planktotrophic larvae for dispersal and feeding.

At 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the reproductive output of a large female Pisaster ochraceus is substantial and has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions. At a body weight of 400 grams, a female can produce approximately 109,589 eggs per day [R400 = approximately 109,589 at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] eggs per day]. This high daily fecundity is a reflection of the species' reproductive strategy, which involves the annual release of gametes during late spring spawning events when water temperatures typically range from 12 to 13 °C. The rate recorded at a body weight of 400 grams derives from field measurements of gonad volume and fecundity estimates, and it places the ochre sea star among the more prolific of the intertidal forcipulatid asteroids. A gravid individual of this size allocates considerable resources to the production of thousands of small, nutrient-rich ova that are broadcast into the water column. The synchrony of gamete release with optimal thermal conditions ensures high fertilisation success and the subsequent development of planktonic larvae. The timing of spawning is tightly linked to seasonal phytoplankton blooms, which provide the first food source for the newly hatched bipinnaria larvae.

The ecological role of Pisaster ochraceus as a keystone predator in the intertidal zone is intimately tied to its massive body size and long lifespan. A large adult with an ultimate wet weight of 1200 grams [Wwi = 1200 grams] exerts significant predation pressure on mussel beds, particularly Mytilus californianus, helping to maintain rocky shore biodiversity. The species' maximum recorded longevity of 34 years [am = 34 years] allows it to exert this top-down control over multiple decades, creating a stable competitive environment for other sessile organisms at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Comparative studies with smaller congeneric species, such as Pisaster giganteus, indicate that the ochre sea star's larger adult size and longer lifespan are correlated with a delayed onset of reproduction, as indicated by the total length at puberty of 5.9 centimeters [Lp = 5.9 centimeters]. The wet weight at birth of 0.0142 grams [Wwb = 0.0142 grams] is minuscule compared to the adult mass, representing a staggering increase of nearly five orders of magnitude over the life course. This dramatic ontogenetic trajectory highlights the efficiency with which these echinoderms convert benthic prey biomass into somatic and reproductive tissue, sustaining their role as dominant predators for decades on end.
